definition: Arboreal means relating to trees, or living in and among them.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word arboreal. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know arboreal should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Tree frogs are thoroughly arboreal, spending nearly their whole lives on leaves and branches high above the forest floor.
A wooded place merely has trees standing in it, while an arboreal creature actually lives up in them.
An arboreal animal lives among the branches, but an epiphytic plant goes further, growing directly on a tree's bark and never touching soil at all.

Tree-dwelling states the plain fact that an animal makes its home in trees, and it stops there. Arboreal covers the same ground but stretches further, describing anything of or about trees - arboreal surveys, arboreal adaptations - and carries a scientific register. Every arboreal monkey is tree-dwelling, but a report on the park's trees is arboreal, not tree-dwelling.

Sylvan means belonging to the woods and is mostly poetic, describing leafy settings and scenery - a sylvan glade, a sylvan path. Arboreal is the plain scientific word for life lived up in the trees themselves. Sylvan sets a leafy scene; arboreal describes a creature whose whole existence happens in the branches.

Arboreal means relating to trees, or living in and among them.
A three-toed sloth is born in the branches, feeds on the leaves within reach, sleeps hooked to a limb, and descends to the ground only once every week or so.
Its curved claws grip bark easily but make walking on flat earth clumsy and slow.
Even its fur grows in the direction that sheds rain while the animal hangs upside down.
Every part of the sloth fits an arboreal life.
The sloth's body and daily routine are built for living in trees rather than on the ground, which is what arboreal describes.
formal, scientific (biology) register
Arboreal most often describes animals and their habits, as in 'arboreal snakes' or 'an arboreal lifestyle,' and it stands in contrast to terrestrial, meaning ground-dwelling.
It can also describe anything of or about trees, as in 'the park's arboreal survey.'

The sloth is built for a life spent almost entirely off the ground.
Its curved claws work like hooks, letting it hang from branches for hours without effort, and its grip stays strong even in sleep.
Field guides describe the species as arboreal, and the label is nearly absolute: a sloth may descend just once a week.
On the forest floor it can barely walk, dragging itself forward by its front claws.
Up in the canopy, though, the slowest mammal on Earth is exactly where it belongs.
